extracted.intended_audience: LaTeX/TikZ users creating technical or scientific graphics (researchers, authors, graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and assembling TikZ graphics for scientific papers/presentations, including node-based diagrams (e.g., Petri nets), labeling, layered backgrounds, snaked connectors, and general graphic design workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Load required TikZ libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Load the specific TikZ/pgf libraries needed for the features you use (e.g., arrow tips, snake, backgrounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \usetikzlibrary{arrows,snakes,backgrounds}. The libraries provide additional definitions (like arrow tips or snake paths) that are not loaded by default and must be explicitly loaded when those features are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer nodes over explicit coordinates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nodes instead of hand-placing many coordinates; nodes preserve the structure of the diagram and make later changes easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: easier to change layout (adding places/transitions doesn't require recomputing coordinates), code becomes more readable and conveys semantic structure (e.g., 'three places and two transitions'). Example: use \node at (0,2) [circle,draw] {} rather than drawing circles at explicit coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose node shapes semantically
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick node shapes according to the semantic role (e.g., circle for Petri-net places, rectangle for transitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A node of shape=circle will be drawn as a circle, shape=rectangle gives a rectangle, etc. You may omit 'shape=' and simply write [circle,draw] if unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the \node / node at syntax for placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Place nodes using 'node at (x,y) [...]' or the shorthand '\node at (x,y) [...] {}' rather than constructing a path of move-tos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The \node form is clearer and avoids creating superfluous move-to operations in a \path. It is the recommended, more readable syntax for placing nodes directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define and use styles to separate semantics from appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Create tikzstyle (or style) definitions for semantic elements so code expresses meaning rather than raw visual attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example styles: \tikzstyle{place}=[circle,draw=blue!50,fill=blue!20,thick] and \tikzstyle{transition}=[rectangle,draw=black!50,fill=black!20,thick]. Using styles makes code communicate 'there are three places and two transitions' rather than listing colors/fills repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control node size with minimum_size and inner_sep
rubrics_metrics.description: Use minimum size (or minimum height/width) and inner sep to set node sizes consistently; prefer minimum size over increasing inner sep globally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set inner sep=0pt together with minimum size to ensure nodes really have the specified size (e.g., inner sep=0pt,minimum size=6mm). inner sep is the automatic padding around text; minimum size ensures consistent node dimensions even with empty text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name nodes for later reference and follow naming rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Give nodes names so you can reference them for anchors/edges/backgrounds; avoid commas, periods, parentheses, colons and other special characters but underscores and hyphens are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two naming methods: the name= option or placing the name in parentheses after the node operation (e.g., \node[place] (waiting) at (0,2) {};). Naming improves code readability and allows coordinate-based references like (node.anchor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relative placement (below of/right of/left of) and node_distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer placing nodes relative to others (below of=..., right of=...) with node distance controlling spacing, rather than absolute coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relative placement yields code that scales and moves better and is easier for others to read. The node distance is between node centers, not borders. Example: \node[place, below of=waiting] {}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add labels next to nodes via explicit label or auxiliary node
rubrics_metrics.description: Attach labels to nodes either by creating another node at an anchor (e.g., above of node.north) or using the label option (label=above:$s\le3$).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: label option constructs a second node next to the target node; you can give multiple label options for multiple labels. To style labels, redefine the every label style or use label={[red]above:...} (note the braces required to avoid closing the outer option list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect nodes using anchors or let TikZ pick anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use anchors like (node.west) or simply use node names (e.g., (enter_critical) -- (critical)) and let TikZ choose a border anchor automatically when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When TikZ sees a whole node name as a coordinate, it heuristically selects a border anchor depending on the path; use explicit anchors when automatic choice is incorrect. Example explicit: \draw[->] (critical.west) -- (enter_critical.east); implicit: \draw[->] (enter_critical) -- (critical);

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'to' operation with in/out or bend options for curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'to' with options like in, out, or bend right/left to control how curves leave/arrive, instead of manually specifying control points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \draw (waiting) to [out=180,in=90] (enter_critical); or \draw (waiting) to [bend right=45] (enter_critical); this simplifies curve specification and improves readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the edge operation to create edges that are added after the main path
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'edge' when building node-centric paths; edges created with edge are not part of the main path and can each have their own arrow tips and colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows writing multiple edges in a compact way attached to a node, each with independent options (e.g., edge [->], edge [<-,bend left=45] (waiting), edge [->,bend right=45] (semaphore);).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define reusable edge styles and set global bend angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Create styles for common edge types (e.g., pre/post) and set a global bend angle to avoid repeating numeric bend values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \tikzstyle{pre}=[<-,shorten <=1pt,>=stealth',semithick] and \tikzstyle{post}=[->,shorten >=1pt,>=stealth',semithick]; then use \begin{tikzpicture}[bend angle=45] to apply consistent bends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place labels on lines automatically with auto and swap
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the auto option to position labels next to curves/lines and swap to mirror placement across the line, enabling placement of multiple labels on a single to operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \draw (a) to node {1} node[swap] {1'} (b); auto moves nodes off the curve next to it, useful in complex plots for consistent label placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the snake library for repeating patterned connectors
rubrics_metrics.description: For snake-like connectors (bumpy or saw-tooth patterns), use snake=snake and tune parameters such as segment_amplitude, segment_length, and line_after_snake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \draw[->,snake=snake,segment amplitude=.4mm,segment length=2mm,line after snake=1mm] (0,0) -- (3,0); adjust parameters to ensure snake ends/starts don't overlap arrowheads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typeset multiline text on paths using text width and centered alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding multi-line text (e.g., above a path), specify text width and center alignment to allow line breaking and neat centering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: node [above,text width=3cm,text centered,midway] {replacement of the capacity by two places}; specifying text width enables automatic line breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use layers (background library) to draw background elements after main content
rubrics_metrics.description: Place background shapes (e.g., rectangles behind groups) in a background layer using {pgfonlayer}{background} so they are drawn behind the main content and can refer to finished node coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw background elements after nodes exist so you can reference node coordinates for corners. Example: \begin{pgfonlayer}{background} \filldraw ... (semaphore.south -| enter_critical.west) rectangle (waiting.north -| leave_critical.east); \end{pgfonlayer}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse existing domain-specific TikZ libraries when available
rubrics_metrics.description: If a library (e.g., the Petri-net library) already defines styles and options you need, use it rather than reimplementing everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using libraries can shorten code and provide familiar conventions (e.g., \tikzstyle{every place}, \tikzstyle{every transition}). You may still override colors or specific options as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide explicitly what the graphic should communicate
rubrics_metrics.description: Before designing, determine the purpose and the single message(s) the graphic should convey to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make this a conscious decision: 'What is the graphic supposed to tell the reader?' This guides which details to include and which to omit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch an outline/rough draft before finalizing details
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a rough overall shape of the graphic (often by pencil and paper) showing crucial elements, then fill in details to make a first draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the graphic creation process like writing: outline → first draft → revisions. A rough sketch helps focus on information hierarchy and layout before spending time on fine details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise graphics iteratively along with the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise the graphic repeatedly as the paper evolves; final graphics typically require several rounds of refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphics, like text, benefit from multiple revisions. Integrate graphic revision into the overall paper revision process rather than leaving graphics as an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and budget sufficient time for creating graphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a graphic takes as much time to create as an equivalent amount of text; plan time accordingly and treat graphics as first-class citizens of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb from the text: about half an hour for a first draft of a half-page graphic; later 1–2 hours (or more) for revisions. Difficult, high-information-density graphics may require significantly more time; don't expect 'five minutes' quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether general guidelines apply to your situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before blindly following a guideline, ask whether it addresses your specific situation and whether breaking it intentionally yields a net benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two diagnostic questions offered: 1) Does this guideline really address my situation? 2) If you do the opposite, will the advantages outweigh the disadvantages the guideline was meant to prevent? The basic typographic rule: 'Every rule can be broken, as long as you are aware that you are breaking a rule.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide inline vs standalone placement and be aware of LaTeX figure drift
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the graphic should be inlined within text or placed as a standalone figure; be mindful LaTeX may place floating figures away from their referencing text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document notes printers/editors like filled pages and LaTeX encourages drifting of standalone figures for technical reasons; choose placement to balance readability and production constraints.
